body: Timeline Seven centuries of history 814 → 146 From the Phoenician foundation to the Roman capture: the key dates of Carthage, era by era. 32 events 4 major periods Major periods Archaic period 814–550 Golden age 550–264 Punic Wars 264–201 Capture & continuity 201–146 814 BC The width of each period is proportional to its length 146 BC 814–550 BC Archaic period Foundation and growth of the city. Carthage evolves from a simple Phoenician trading post into the dominant metropolis of the western Mediterranean, at the head of a vast network of colonies and trading posts. 550–264 BC Golden age The peak of Carthaginian power: naval dominance, wars against the Greeks of Sicily, scientific agriculture and continental-scale trade. 264–201 BC Punic Wars The titanic clash with Rome for mastery of the Mediterranean, marked by Hannibal Barca's epic campaigns in Italy. 201–146 BC Capture & continuity After Zama, Carthage enjoys a remarkable economic revival. In 146, Rome takes the city by force; but Punic culture, language and people outlive it. Key dates All biographies → All · 32 Foundation & expansion · 14 Punic Wars · 12 Fall · 6 814 – 264 BC Foundation & expansion From a colony of Tyre to the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean. 814 BC Foundation of Carthage Phoenician princess Dido (Elissa), fleeing Tyre after her husband Sychaeus was murdered by her brother Pygmalion, founds Carthage — Qart Hadasht, "New City" — on the coast of present-day Tunisia. The hill of Byrsa becomes the heart of the city. The date comes from the Greek historian Timaeus; the oldest excavated remains go back to the second half of the 8th century BC. The foundation → Dido → Foundation 7th c. BC Mediterranean expansion Carthage establishes trading posts in Sardinia, western Sicily, the Balearics — Ibiza (Ebusus) is founded around 654 according to Diodorus — and along the North African coast. It becomes the leading Phoenician power in the western Mediterranean. Animated map → Expansion 535 BC Battle of Alalia Allied with the Etruscans, the Carthaginians fight the Phocaean Greeks off Corsica. According to Herodotus, the Phocaeans win but lose 40 of their 60 ships and abandon the island: a strategic victory for Carthage, which checks Greek expansion in the western Mediterranean. Battle 509 BC First treaty with Rome Recorded by Polybius, this treaty of trade and non-aggression sets out spheres of influence: Roman ships may not sail beyond the "Fair Promontory" near Carthage. The young Republic recognises Punic maritime supremacy. The economy → Diplomacy 480 BC Battle of Himera In Sicily, Hamilcar the Magonid is defeated by Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas. The setback halts Carthaginian expansion on the island for decades and triggers political reforms in Carthage. Battle 5th c. BC The voyages of Hanno and Himilco Hanno sails down the Atlantic coast of Africa with a fleet of colonists; Himilco explores the Atlantic coasts of Europe. Hanno's account, translated into Greek, has come down to us. Hanno → Animated map → Exploration 5th c. BC Carthage turns towards Africa According to Justin, Carthage had paid the Africans a yearly rent for the ground of the city since its foundation; under the Magonids it stops paying and subdues its hinterland. This has been seen as a consequence of Himera; some historians prefer to speak of a gradual expansion. The foundation → Africa 409–405 BC Return to Sicily Hannibal, Hamilcar's grandson, destroys Selinus and Himera (409). He dies of plague before Akragas, which his successor Himilco takes (406). The peace made with Dionysius of Syracuse (405) is no more than a truce. The Punic Wars → War 398–396 BC Dionysius of Syracuse against Carthage Dionysius takes Motya, the Punic stronghold of western Sicily. The Carthaginian counter-attack leads to the siege of Syracuse, lifted in 396 because of an epidemic. War resumes on and off for sixty years. War 348 BC Second treaty with Rome Reported by Polybius (III, 24), it extends the zone closed to the Romans as far as Mastia in Spain, and shuts Sardinia and Libya to them. The Punic Wars → Diplomacy 310 BC Agathocles invades Africa The tyrant of Syracuse lands on Cape Bon and directly threatens Carthage. He is eventually driven out (307), but the invasion exposes the vulnerability of the city's African territory. War 306 BC The “Philinus treaty” According to the historian Philinus of Akragas, Rome and Carthage barred themselves from Sicily and Italy respectively. Polybius disputes that this treaty existed; Livy records a renewal of the alliance that year. The question is still debated. The Punic Wars → Diplomacy 279 BC Alliance against Pyrrhus Rome and Carthage agree to help each other against Pyrrhus, king of Epirus (Polybius, III, 25). It is their last treaty before the war. label: Carthage lives in Tunisia
title: Carthage lives in Tunisia
desc: The city of Elissa and Hannibal gave Tunisia its first great state, and gave the world the very name of Africa.
headings: From colonial villa to presidential palace
body: قرطاج Tunisia · 3,000 years of history Carthage lives in Tunisia The city of Elissa and Hannibal gave Tunisia its first great state, and gave the world the very name of Africa. Byrsa Hill and the Gulf of Tunis — UNESCO site since 1979 One name, four languages 𐤒𐤓𐤕𐤇𐤃𐤔𐤕 Qart-Ḥadasht Phoenician-Punic: "New City". The original name, around 814 BC. Καρχηδών Karchēdṓn The Greek name, used by Polybius and the Hellenistic authors. CARTHAGO Carthago The Latin, source of Carthage, Carthagena and Cartagena. قرطاج Qarṭāj Arabic: today a municipality in the northern suburbs of Tunis. Where does the word "Africa" come from? Africa was born in Tunisia The Afri The Romans called the people of the Carthage region Afri . 146 BC After the fall of Carthage, Rome created the province of Africa , covering the north-east of present-day Tunisia. 7th c. The name becomes إفريقية Ifriqiya , with Kairouan as its capital: Tunisia and its borderlands. Today The name of a Tunisian region now designates an entire continent of 54 countries. The origin of the word Afri is still debated: suggestions include the Berber ifri ("cave"), the Phoenician ʿafar ("dust") or the name of a tribe. Africa and its name → Kairouan , capital of Ifriqiya — the Great Mosque (7th–9th c.) The name Carthage today Twenty-two centuries after 146 BC, the name remains the symbol of Tunisia. State Carthage Palace Seat of the presidency of the Tunisian Republic. Travel Tunis–Carthage Airport The country's main gateway. Cinema · since 1966 Carthage Film Festival The oldest film festival in Africa and the Arab world. Music · since 1964 Carthage International Festival Every summer, in the ancient theatre of Carthage. Sport The Eagles of Carthage The nickname of the national football team. Learning University of Carthage One of the country's major public universities. Stage Carthage Theatre Days The great meeting place of Arab and African theatre. Heritage 9 Tunisian sites on the UNESCO list, including Carthage, Kerkouane, Dougga and Kairouan. A Tunisian continuity Punic Carthage 814 – 146 BC Roman Africa Carthage refounded, second city of the West Ifriqiya Kairouan, Mahdia, Tunis Tunis Hafsids, the beylik Tunisia Independence in 1956 — Carthage as an emblem The town Carthage, a town of today A residential municipality of Greater Tunis, built in the middle of the archaeological site. 17,010 inhabitants in the 2014 census (National Institute of Statistics). 1919 the municipality is created by a beylical decree of 15 June. 3 districts: Carthage, Carthage-Mohamed Ali (created in 1983) and El Yasmina. 15 km from central Tunis, with about 3 km of coast on the gulf, between Le Kram to the south and Sidi Bou Saïd to the north. Names that tell the past The neighbourhoods Salammbô Around the Punic ports and the tophet. Minister Mustapha Khaznadar built the first summer palace here in the 19th century; the National Institute of Marine Sciences and Technologies (1924) has its oceanographic museum here. Byrsa The historic hill: National Museum of Carthage, the Acropolium (the former cathedral) and the Punic quarter. Carthage-Présidence Around the presidential palace; Le Corbusier built the Villa Baizeau here (1928–1929), and the Carthage-Présidence high school dates from 1952. Douar Chott · La Malga The two farming hamlets that survived before the 19th century; they hold the Roman circus and the great cisterns. Dermech, Hannibal, Amilcar TGM stations and residential areas; the last two bear the names of great Carthaginians. Mohamed Ali · El Yasmina The newest areas, which became districts as the population grew. Carthage Palace From colonial villa to presidential palace The first European-style villas appear around 1906. The largest belongs to the secretary-general of the Tunisian government, the French official who actually ran the administration of the protectorate. In 1960 Bourguiba turns it into the presidential palace, on the shore, a stone’s throw from the Antonine Baths. Carthage is not the capital, but it has become an “emblematic seat of power” (Sophie Bessis), while Tunis keeps the administration and the economy. Among the town’s mayors: Chedli Klibi (1963–1990) and Fouad Mebazaa (1995–1998). Learning and culture A town of institutions National Museum (in the former White Fathers’ buildings), the Acropolium and its Jazz à Carthage festival (since 2005), the Tunisian Academy Beit al-Hikma in the Zarrouk palace (since 1983), IHEC Carthage, the Malik ibn Anas Mosque (2003, 55 m minaret, room for over 1,000 worshippers). Transport Six TGM stations The TGM train crosses the town, linking it to La Goulette and Tunis on one side and to Sidi Bou Saïd and La Marsa on the other: Salammbô, Byrsa, Dermech, Hannibal, Présidence and Amilcar stations. Transtu buses also run to Ariana and Tunis. label: The victors' history
title: History written by the victor — Carthage
desc: Almost everything we read about Carthage was written by its enemies. What Rome said, and what we know.
headings: What Rome said / what we know
body: Sources & re-readings History written by the victor Almost everything we read about Carthage was written by its enemies. Rome never got over Cannae; it told the story of Carthage its own way. Scipio "Africanus" — the victor took the name of the vanquished 0 Carthaginian history books have come down to us 1 Punic author translated by Rome: Mago, because his treatise on agriculture was useful to it 6,000+ Punic inscriptions recovered by archaeology, mostly religious What Rome said / what we know Roman account What we know THE ROMAN ACCOUNT THE STATE OF KNOWLEDGE "Punica fides" "Punic faith" became a Latin byword for treachery. Livy credits Hannibal with "more than Punic perfidy". A propaganda insult Carthage signed and honoured treaties with Rome for centuries. In 149, it was Rome that changed its demands once the city had disarmed. Salt on the ruins Rome supposedly sowed salt so that nothing would ever grow again. A modern myth No ancient text mentions it: the story appears in European writers of the 19th–20th centuries. Rome in fact refounded Carthage a century later. Merchants without culture Carthage supposedly knew only trade — no art, no literature. Scattered libraries According to Pliny, in 146 Rome gave the libraries of Carthage to the Numidian kings. Their contents are lost — an absence of books is not an absence of culture. A people of sacrifice Diodorus and Plutarch describe systematic child sacrifice. An open debate Archaeologists remain divided over the tophet: some see sacrifice there, others mainly a cemetery for infants who died of natural causes. The tophet and the gods of Carthage → Antiquity Partisan authors Polybius was the friend of Scipio Aemilianus, who destroyed Carthage. Livy, writing under Augustus, produced a history to the glory of Rome, in which defeats are explained by the enemy's cunning. 19th century The colonial gaze Europe identified with "civilising" Rome and turned Carthage into a barbarous Orient — the image of Flaubert's Salammbô (1862), shortly before the French protectorate of 1881. Today Giving Carthage back its voice The UNESCO "Save Carthage" campaign (1972–1995), Tunisian scholars and international excavations are rebuilding the city from its own traces. label: The founding
title: The foundation of Carthage — 814 BC
desc: Elissa flees Tyre, the oxhide trick, the hill of Byrsa: the foundation of Carthage between legend and archaeology, its twin harbour, its walls and its crafts.
headings: Before Carthage: the western Phoenician network
A confederation rather than an empire
An ideal site, a planned city
body: 𐤒𐤓𐤕𐤇𐤃𐤔𐤕 814 BC The foundation of Carthage Birth of a Mediterranean superpower: a princess in exile, an oxhide, a hill facing the sea. J. M. W. Turner, Dido building Carthage (1815) 814 Traditional year of foundation (BC) 700,000 Inhabitants at its peak according to Strabo — probably an exaggeration 34 km Of city walls, according to ancient writers 220 Warships housed in the circular harbour 6 Storeys of the houses on the slopes of Byrsa, according to Appian 300 Elephants stabled inside the walls The legend Elissa, princess of Tyre Dido (Elissa) was a Phoenician princess from Tyre, in present-day Lebanon. Her brother Pygmalion, king of Tyre, murdered her husband Sychaeus — a wealthy priest of the temple of Melqart, the Phoenician Hercules — to seize his treasure. Her husband's ghost warned her in a dream. She fled by sea with a group of loyal followers and Sychaeus's riches. During a stop in Cyprus, 80 young women joined the expedition; she reached the coast of present-day Tunisia around 814 BC. There she negotiated with the Libyan (Berber) king Iarbas for land: as much as a single oxhide could cover — a seemingly modest request. According to the legend, when later pressed to marry Iarbas, she chose to throw herself onto a pyre. The life of Dido → Pierre-Narcisse Guérin, Aeneas telling Dido of the misfortunes of Troy (1815), Louvre Sources The story comes to us from Greek and Latin writers — Timaeus, Justin (epitome of Pompeius Trogus), Virgil. The meeting with Aeneas is a poetic invention of the Aeneid: the dates do not match. History written by the victor → The oxhide stratagem How Dido founded Carthage by cunning. 01 The request Dido asks Iarbas for as much land as an oxhide can cover. The king, thinking it trivial, agrees. 02 The trick She has the hide cut into extremely thin strips, forming a very long leather cord. 03 The foundation With these strips she encircles the whole hill of Byrsa — from the Greek "byrsa", hide. There she founds Qart Hadasht, the "New City". 04 The growth From this hill, Carthage grows into one of the greatest cities of the ancient world, with a naval harbour for 220 ships. Myth and archaeology What the excavations say 814 / 813 Foundation date given by the Greek historian Timaeus of Tauromenium (4th–3rd c. BC) and taken up by tradition. Appian Another ancient tradition, followed by Appian (Libyca, I, 1), dated Carthage to the time of the Trojan War, around the 12th century BC. Excavation has found nothing that old. Hypotheses Some scholars proposed a foundation around 670, or a two-stage one — first a trading post, then the city proper (Pierre Cintas). Recent historians, relying on the annals of Tyre known through Menander of Ephesus and Flavius Josephus, favour the last quarter of the 9th century. 8th c. The oldest excavated layers — pottery, the first offerings in the tophet of Salammbô — date to the second half of the 8th century BC: the legend is not far from the truth. Byrsa The Greek name "byrsa" (hide) is probably a reinterpretation of a Semitic word for the citadel: the oxhide trick may have grown out of this pun. 6th c. Carthage takes the lead of the western Phoenician cities, while Tyre falls under Babylonian, then Persian rule. Full timeline → A name 𐤒𐤓𐤕𐤇𐤃𐤔𐤕 Qart Hadasht, the "New City" In Phoenician, qart means "city" and hadasht "new": a new Tyre in Africa. The Greeks made it Karchēdōn, the Romans Carthago — and the name still lives on in Tunisia. Cartagena, in Spain, bore the same name, Qart Hadasht. Carthage and Tunisia → Before Carthage: the western Phoenician network For the Phoenicians, North Africa was at first a stopover on the route to the metals of Spain. Carthage joined a network that was already old. Tunisia 1101 Utica According to Pliny the Elder (Natural History, XVI, 216), the first Phoenician foundation in Africa, almost three centuries before Carthage. This is a traditional date: the oldest remains found are considerably later. Atlantic Morocco 12th c. Lixus Beyond the Strait of Gibraltar, near modern Larache. Pliny (XIX, 63) counts it among the oldest Phoenician settlements; it later came into the orbit of Carthage. Spain c. 1100 Gades (Gadir) Modern Cádiz, on an island. Velleius Paterculus (I, 2, 3) dates its foundation by the Tyrians shortly after the Trojan War. It opened access to the silver and tin of the Iberian Peninsula. Head of the network 6th c. A confederation rather than an empire As Tyre declined, Carthage took the lead of the western Phoenician colonies and handled their common defence and foreign policy. Sabatino Moscati saw this loose structure as one of the causes of its final defeat. The Libyan substratum A land already inhabited The Phoenicians did not land on empty ground. North Africa was home to the Libyans, whom Egyptian texts already call Libu at the end of the 2nd millennium BC. For Gabriel Camps they are the ancestors of the Berbers; they were not a single people but a patchwork of tribes. Settlement was nego

label: The Punic Wars
title: The Punic Wars (264–146 BC) — Carthage
desc: The three wars between Carthage and Rome: Mylae, Ecnomus, the Aegates, the Mercenary War, Hannibal, Cannae, Zama, the siege of 149–146, the treaties and indemnities.
headings: Before Rome: the Greeks of Sicily
Two centuries of struggle for Sicily
body: 264–146 BC The Punic Wars Three wars in a hundred and eighteen years: the duel between Carthage and Rome for the Mediterranean. The word comes from the Latin punicus, "Phoenician" — Rome’s name for the Carthaginians. J. Trumbull — The Death of Paulus Aemilius at Cannae (1773) 3 wars between Carthage and Rome 118 years from the start of the first (264) to the fall of Carthage (146) 43 years of open war in total (23 + 17 + 3) 10,000 talents of silver imposed on Carthage in 201, payable over 50 years Before the Punic Wars Before Rome: the Greeks of Sicily For more than two centuries Carthage's enemy was not Rome but the Greek cities, above all in Sicily. With Rome, relations were long governed by treaties. The Sicilian wars Two centuries of struggle for Sicily c. 540–535 Alalia. Allied with the Etruscans, the Carthaginians fight the Phocaean Greeks off Corsica. Victorious on paper, the Phocaeans lose most of their fleet and leave the island (Herodotus, I, 166). 480 Himera. Gelon of Syracuse, allied with Theron of Akragas, seeks to unite Greek Sicily. The army of Hamilcar the Magonid is crushed; Carthage may have had the backing of Persia, which attacked Greece the same year. 409–405 The return. Hannibal, Hamilcar's grandson, destroys Selinus and Himera (409). He dies of plague before Akragas; his successor Himilco takes the city, then makes a peace with Dionysius of Syracuse that is no more than a truce. 398–396 Dionysius. Dionysius captures Motya, the great Punic stronghold in the west of the island, which Carthage later retakes. The Carthaginian siege of Syracuse has to be lifted in 396 because of an epidemic. c. 340 The Punic west. After sixty years of intermittent war and the defeat at the Crimisus against Timoleon, Carthage holds only the west and south-west of the island. 315–307 Agathocles. The tyrant of Syracuse takes Messana, then attacks the Punic posts. Besieged in Syracuse, he carries the war to Africa (see below). 278–276 Pyrrhus. Called in by the Sicilian Greeks, the king of Epirus takes almost all the Punic strongholds but fails before Lilybaeum, then leaves the island. Diplomacy The treaties with Rome 509/508 The first treaty. Preserved by Polybius (III, 22), who dates it to the first consuls. The Romans must not sail beyond the “Fair Promontory”; Carthage undertakes not to harm the Latin cities. 348 The second treaty. Reported by Polybius (III, 24) and dated by Diodorus and Livy. The zone closed to the Romans extends to Spain (Mastia); Sardinia and Libya are shut to them. 306 ? The “Philinus treaty”. According to the historian Philinus of Akragas, Rome renounced Sicily and Carthage Italy. Polybius (III, 26) denies it ever existed; Livy mentions a renewal in 306. The debate remains open. 279/278 Against Pyrrhus. The two cities agree to help each other against the king of Epirus (Polybius, III, 25). It is their last agreement before the war. These treaties guaranteed Carthage a monopoly of trade in North Africa and Rome the security of Latium. Their ever closer rhythm is often read as a sign of rising tension. 310–307 BC Agathocles in Africa In 310 Hamilcar, son of Gisco, holds almost all of Sicily and besieges Syracuse. Agathocles breaks the blockade, lands on Cape Bon and burns his ships to deprive his soldiers of any hope of retreat (Diodorus, XX). For the first time an enemy army ravages Carthage's African territory, and several of its Libyan subjects defect. Carthage has to recall its troops from Sicily. The war lasts three years and ends with the flight of Agathocles, who abandons his army (307). 278–276 BC Pyrrhus in Sicily After his costly victories over Rome in Italy, the king of Epirus crosses to Sicily at the call of the Greeks. He takes Eryx and nearly all the Punic west, but is stopped at Lilybaeum, which his fleet cannot blockade. He leaves in 276, predicting, according to Plutarch, that he was leaving Sicily as a battlefield for the Romans and Carthaginians. Twelve years later the First Punic War broke out. Three wars A war for Sicily, a war for the Mediterranean, a war to destroy Carthage. 264–241 BC First Punic War The struggle for Sicily Cause Messana calls on Rome for help; Rome crosses the strait into Sicily, Carthage’s sphere. Battles Mylae, Ecnomus, Tunis, Drepana, the Aegates Islands Outcome Roman victory: Carthage evacuates Sicily. Details ↓ 218–201 BC Second Punic War Hannibal’s war Cause Hannibal takes Saguntum, Rome’s ally in Spain (219). Battles Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae, Metaurus, Zama Outcome Roman victory: Carthage loses Spain and its fleet. Details ↓ 149–146 BC Third Punic War The siege of Carthage Cause Carthage defends itself against Masinissa without Rome’s consent (150). Battles Three years of siege, the assault of spring 146 Outcome Carthage is taken and burned; its territory becomes the province of Africa. label: The Mercenary War
title: The Mercenary War (241–237 BC) — the “truceless” war — Carthage
desc: The Mercenary War, or “truceless” war (Polybius I, 65–88): unpaid wages, Spendius, Mathos and Autaritus, the Libyan uprising, the Bagradas, the torture of Gisco, the pass of the Saw, the loss of Sardinia and Flaubert’s novel Salammbô.
headings: When the army turns on the city
A victory that paved the way for the next war
Salammbô, the novel of the war
A novel faithful to Polybius… but for its heroine
body: The battle of the Macar (the Bagradas), watercolour by Georges Rochegrosse for an edition of Salammbô, c. 1900 (Musée des Beaux-Arts, Rouen). Punic Wars · Africa ἄσπονδος πόλεμος 241 – 237 BC The Mercenary War The “truceless” war — Carthage against its own army Just defeated by Rome, Carthage cannot pay the soldiers who fought for it in Sicily. Their anger, soon taken up by Libyan peasants crushed by taxes, sets Punic Africa ablaze for more than three years. Polybius saw it as the most atrocious war he knew of. 20,000+ mercenaries gathered at Tunis at the start of the revolt Polybius, I, 67 ~70,000 Libyans join the insurgents at Mathos’ call Polybius, I, 73 40,000+ rebels killed at the pass of the Saw, out of about 50,000 Polybius, I, 84–85 40 months of war: “three years and about four months” Polybius, I, 88 An African civil war When the army turns on the city Carthage, a trading city with few citizens, fought its wars with soldiers from elsewhere: Iberians, Celts, Ligurians, Balearic islanders, “half-barbarian” Greeks and above all Libyans from its own territory. In 241 the peace of Lutatius ended the First Punic War; these men had to be brought back from Sicily and paid years of arrears. But the treasury was empty: the war had ruined the city, which also owed Rome 3,200 talents. Haggling turned into mutiny, mutiny into war, and the war into an uprising of the whole of Africa against its capital. Polybius calls it the war “without truce” (ἄσπονδος), rendered in French as “inexpiable”: no convention, no mercy was respected. It brought Hamilcar Barca and his family to the fore, and it cost Carthage Sardinia. The sources An almost unique account Polybius — Histories, I, 65–88: the only continuous, detailed account, written a century later from lost sources. Diodorus Siculus — Library of History, book XXV: fragments, dwelling on the atrocities. Appian — Libyca, 5: a brief mention, mainly of the Sardinian affair. Cornelius Nepos — Life of Hamilcar, 2: the revolt and Hamilcar’s victory in a few lines. All these authors wrote on the winners’ side, Roman or Greek. We know the revolt only through them — and through the coins struck by the insurgents themselves. The causes Unpaid wages, a political blunder and an Africa at the end of its tether. Lilybaeum, 241 Gisco’s caution Commander at Lilybaeum, Gisco sent the mercenaries back from Sicily in small groups so that each could be paid and discharged separately. But Carthage, short of money, let them pile up in the city, then sent them all together to Sicca with their baggage. Sicca, 241 Hanno’s blunder Hanno — usually identified with Hanno “the Great”, leader of the landowners’ party — came to Sicca to ask the soldiers to accept reduced pay. None of them spoke the same language; rumour did the rest. More than 20,000 men marched on Tunis, at the gates of Carthage. The countryside The anger of the Libyans During the war with Rome, Carthage had taken half of the Libyan peasants’ harvests and doubled the towns’ taxes. When Mathos called them to revolt they rose en masse; the women, says Polybius, gave their jewellery to fund the war. The protagonists Rebel leaders from all over the Mediterranean world against Carthage’s rival generals. On the rebel side Campanian Spendius A runaway slave of the Romans, he feared being handed back to his masters if peace was made. A skilled speaker, he drove the army to the break. Crucified before Tunis. Libyan Mathos A free man compromised in the first disturbances. He turned the mutiny into a Libyan war of liberation and became the revolt’s most enduring leader. Captured in 237. Gaul Autaritus Leader of the Celts; he spoke Punic, which made him heard by all. With Spendius he had the killing of Gisco voted. Captured at the Saw. Libyan Zarzas Leader of a Libyan contingent, he joined Spendius and Autaritus in the last campaign and was among the envoys detained by Hamilcar at the Saw. On the Carthaginian side The negotiator Gisco The officer who had organised the repatriation. Sent to Tunis with the money, he was seized by the rebels with his escort, then mutilated and put to death. The first general Hanno Victorious before Utica thanks to more than a hundred elephants, he then let his camp be surprised. His rivalry with Hamilcar long paralysed the command. The saviour Hamilcar Barca Undefeated in Sicily, recalled with 10,000 men and 70 elephants. Strategist of the Bagradas and the Saw, he came out of the war master of the army. The Numidian prince Naravas He went over to Hamilcar with 2,000 horsemen; in return Hamilcar promised him his daughter’s hand — Polybius does not give her name. Gisco sends the mercenaries back to Africa. 241 From Sicca to Tunis — Hanno asks for reduced pay; more than 20,000 soldiers march on Tunis. label: The fall of Carthage
title: The capture of Carthage — 149-146 BC
desc: The Third Punic War: disarmament, a three-year siege, Scipio Aemilianus, the fall of Byrsa, Hasdrubal and his wife, the salt myth and the Roman refoundation.
headings: A real destruction, not an erasure
Masinissa, the other architect of the fall
The triple wall of the isthmus
The citadel, from the last stand to the excavations
"Salt was sown to sterilise the soil"
Carthage taken by sabotage, not destroyed
body: 149 – 146 BC The capture of Carthage What Rome did, and what it claimed to have done: the Third Punic War, from the disarming of the city to the burning of Byrsa. The Punic quarter of Byrsa, burnt in 146 3 years of siege, from 149 to the spring of 146 BC 200,000 suits of armour and 2,000 catapults handed to Rome before the war 6 days and six nights of street fighting up to Byrsa 50,000 survivors who came out of Byrsa, sold into slavery Cato the Elder « Carthago delenda est » Back from an embassy to Africa, struck by Carthage's renewed prosperity, Cato ends every speech in the Senate with this phrase. According to Plutarch, he showed fresh figs picked in Carthage three days earlier: the enemy was within sailing distance. Scipio Nasica, by contrast, argued for sparing the city. The story and the facts A real destruction, not an erasure Rome burnt and dismantled Carthage, and killed or enslaved its people. But the tale of a city "razed" and sterilised with salt is legend: excavations find the Punic city beneath the Roman one, and Punic culture survived for centuries. History written by the victor → Masinissa, the other architect of the fall Rome struck the final blow, but it was the Numidian king Masinissa who, for fifty years, ate away at Carthage's territory and handed Rome its pretext. Coin of Masinissa — British Museum Why? Rich lands, a coveted city Masinissa wanted to build a great settled Numidian kingdom, with towns and wheat-growing land. Yet the most fertile plains and the richest trading posts in Africa belonged to Carthage, whose prosperity had survived defeat. He knew that with Rome behind him, every annexation would go unpunished. Fifty years of pressure, 206 – 148 212 – 206 Raised at Carthage according to Appian, he fights for the city in Hispania against the Scipios. 206 Carthage backs his rival Syphax; Masinissa goes over to Rome. 202 His Numidian cavalry is decisive at Zama: it returns to strike Hannibal's army from behind. 201 The peace treaty lets him claim “the lands of his ancestors” without fixing any boundary, and forbids Carthage to wage any war without Rome's consent: Carthage can no longer defend itself alone. 193 He seizes part of the Emporia, the rich trading posts of the Lesser Syrtis (Livy). Rome sends arbitrators who settle nothing. 174 – 172 Carthage complains to Rome that in two years Masinissa has taken more than 70 of its towns and forts (Livy). 162 – 161 The Emporia are annexed again; Rome rules for Masinissa, and Carthage must also pay him 500 talents (Polybius). 153 – 152 He takes the Great Plains and the Thugga region, some fifty towns (Appian). The Roman embassy sent to arbitrate, Cato among them, returns convinced that Carthage must be destroyed. 150 Pushed to the limit, Carthage raises some 25,000 men under Hasdrubal. Surrounded and starving, the army surrenders; the horsemen of Gulussa, Masinissa's son, massacre the prisoners. For Rome, this is the breach of the 201 treaty it had been waiting for. 148 Masinissa dies at nearly 90, in the middle of the siege of Carthage. Scipio Aemilianus divides his kingdom among his sons. Without Hannibal Carthage had lost its best defender. As suffete, Hannibal had reformed the state and restored its finances, but his enemies denounced him to Rome. He went into exile in 195 and died in 183, long before the last war. An awkward ally Rome used Masinissa without wanting to hand him Carthage. Several modern historians think the destruction of the city was also meant to stop an overly powerful Numidian kingdom from taking it: on his death, his kingdom was immediately divided. The defences of Carthage Before the siege, here is what Rome had to take: a city built on a peninsula, closed on the landward side by one of the most powerful fortifications of the ancient world. They explain how a disarmed city held out for almost three years. Triple line across the isthmus Sea wall (single) Byrsa, citadel Harbours Weak angle (Appian) Schematic reconstruction — lines and proportions approximate, after Polybius and Appian. Appian, Libyca, 95 The triple wall of the isthmus Isthmus About 25 stades wide (≈ 4.5 km) according to Polybius (I, 73) and Appian: the only way in by land. Height 30 cubits (≈ 13 to 14 m) for each wall, not counting parapets and towers. Thickness 30 feet (≈ 9 m). Towers One every two plethra (≈ 60 m), four storeys high. Lower level Stalls for 300 elephants and their food stores. Upper level Stables for 4,000 horses and stores of barley and fodder. Barracks Room for 20,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry. Three identical walls? Appian wrote in the 2nd century AD, drawing on Polybius, who witnessed the siege. Many modern historians read it instead as a defence in depth: a ditch, a palisade or outer wall, then the great towered wall housing barracks and stables. Length 34 km, a figure to qualify The often-quoted figure comes from Livy (Periochae, 51): a circuit of 23 Roman miles, about 34 km. Orosius counts 22 (≈ 32.5 km); Strabo gives 3

headings: Twenty-two centuries on the same hill
Summer palaces, a cathedral and excavations
A town and a World Heritage site
body: 146 BC → today Carthage after Carthage The Punic city burned in 146. On its ruins another Carthage lived for seven centuries, faded away, served as a quarry, and was reborn as a town and a World Heritage site. Antonine Baths, 2nd century — Roman Carthage by the gulf 7 centuries as a Roman, Vandal and Byzantine city, from 29 BC to 698 30,000 seats in the Roman amphitheatre, of which only the arena survives 1979 the archaeological site joins the UNESCO World Heritage List 17,010 inhabitants in the municipality of Carthage (2014 census) Timeline of the ages Twenty-two centuries on the same hill Each age built on top of the last one, or with its stones. Roman era 29 BC – 439 Carthage refounded 122 BC Gaius Gracchus tries to settle a colony, Junonia, near the cursed site; the project dies with him. 44 – 29 BC Decided by Caesar, the refoundation is carried out under Augustus: Colonia Iulia Concordia Carthago rises on the very site of the Punic city. 1st c. Capital of Africa Proconsularis. The top of Byrsa is levelled to carry the forum. 145 – 162 After a great fire, the Antonine Baths are built by the sea (Colette Picard). 3rd – 4th c. Won over to Christianity, the city lives through the persecutions and becomes one of the great spiritual centres of the Latin West. Vandal kingdom 439 – 533 Genseric's capital 439 Genseric's Vandals seize Carthage and make it the seat of their kingdom. 455 The Vandal fleet that sacks Rome sails from Carthage. 5th c. The Arian Vandal kings turn on the Catholic Church of Africa: bishops exiled, churches confiscated. Byzantine era 533 – 698 The Empire returns 533 Belisarius, Justinian's general, retakes the city, which becomes again a prosperous capital and the seat of the government of Africa. Late 6th c. Byzantine Africa is entrusted to an exarch, both civil and military governor, based in Carthage. 610 Heraclius, son of the exarch of Carthage, sails to Constantinople, takes the throne and founds a dynasty there. Arab conquest 698 Tunis takes over 698 Hassan ibn al-Nu‘man takes the city (Grimal). Looted and burned, it is emptied of its people, who are moved to Tunis. 8th c. Tunis becomes the main city and will give the country its name; the name Africa, turned Ifriqiya, will end up designating the whole continent. 10th c. After nearly two centuries of abandonment, the site is settled again in the Fatimid period, according to Gibbon. Middle Ages – 18th century 9th – 19th c. A marble quarry Spolia Columns, capitals and marble slabs are stripped to build mosques, palaces and churches: in Kairouan, in Tunis, and as far as Europe. 1270 Saint Louis lands at Carthage during the Eighth Crusade and dies of dysentery before Tunis. The failure of the expedition closes the age of the Crusades. 16th c. The village of the time — a mosque, a college, some twenty shops and about 500 peasants — is ruined by the Spanish garrison of La Goulette, installed by Charles V. 18th c. Only two farming hamlets occupy the former capital: Douar Chott and La Malga. Beylik and protectorate 1830 – 1956 Summer palaces, a cathedral and excavations 1830 The bey grants France a plot on Byrsa. Louis-Philippe sends an architect to find where Saint Louis died: unable to, he picks the finest viewpoint, where a chapel is built. 19th c. Dignitaries of the beylik make it their summer retreat: Mustapha Khaznadar's palace in Salammbô, the Zarrouk palace, Mustapha Ben Ismaïl's palace (Revault). 1884 – 1890 Under the French protectorate, the Cathedral of Saint Louis crowns Byrsa; it becomes the primatial church of Africa for Cardinal Lavigerie. 1919 A beylical decree of 15 June creates the municipality of Carthage. 1928 – 1929 Le Corbusier builds the Villa Baizeau, his only work in Tunisia. Independent Tunisia 1956 – today A town and a World Heritage site 1960 Bourguiba chooses a colonial-era villa by the sea to become the presidential palace. 1972 As the city spreads, UNESCO launches a major international campaign to save Carthage. 1979 The archaeological site is inscribed on the World Heritage List. 1985 The mayors of Rome and Carthage, Ugo Vetere and Chedli Klibi, sign a symbolic peace treaty ending the Third Punic War. 2003 The Malik ibn Anas Mosque opens on the Odeon Hill. 2nd – 5th century Christian Carthage As the metropolis of Roman Africa, Carthage becomes one of the hearths of Latin Christianity: its writers shape the theological language of the West and its bishops hold many councils. 397 A council of Carthage settles the list of biblical books recognised by the Church of Africa. 411 The Conference of Carthage gathers over 500 Catholic and Donatist bishops; the imperial commissioner Marcellinus condemns Donatism. 484 The Vandal king Huneric summons Catholic and Arian bishops: the meeting opens a new persecution. c. 155 – c. 220 Tertullian Born in Carthage, the first great Christian writer in Latin. label: Wealth and Rome
title: Why Carthage's wealth exasperated Rome
desc: Defeated twice, Carthage always recovered: the indemnities of 241 and 201, the early repayment offer, Cato's figs, the ultimatum of 149. How Carthage's prosperity came to obsess Rome.
headings: The spiral, from the Aegates to 146
The richest city in the world
body: Silver shekel, 213–210 BC — Melqart and the elephant · British Museum Carthage · Wealth & Rome Too rich for Rome Defeated twice, Carthage always rose again. It was its prosperity, far more than its armies, that ended up obsessing Rome. 700,000 inhabitants on the eve of 149 according to Strabo — probably an exaggeration 300 lb of silver a day (≈ 100 kg): the yield of the Baebelo mine for Hannibal, according to Pliny the Elder 10,000 talents of indemnity imposed in 201 BC, over 50 years (≈ 260 tonnes of silver) 10 years later, Carthage offers to pay it all off at once The spiral, from the Aegates to 146 241 The first bill Defeated at the Aegates Islands, Carthage loses Sicily. The treaty set 2,200 talents over twenty years; the Roman people raised it to 3,200 talents over ten (Polybius). 237 The seizure of Sardinia Taking advantage of the Mercenary War, Rome seizes Sardinia and demands 1,200 more talents under threat of war. Polybius himself calls it unjust. 201 A peace to ruin Carthage After Zama: the fleet cut to 10 ships, the elephants surrendered, 100 hostages, no war without Rome's consent, and 10,000 talents of silver to be paid over 50 years. 196 Hannibal as sufete Elected chief magistrate, he attacks the corruption of the oligarchy and shows that public revenue is enough to pay Rome without new taxes (Livy). His enemies denounce him to Rome; he goes into exile in 195. 191 "We can pay it all" According to Livy, Carthage offers to settle the whole remaining indemnity at once. Rome refuses: the debt was also a leash. ~150 Cato's figs Back from an embassy to Africa, Cato drops still-fresh figs in the Senate: the land that grows them, he says, is only three days' sail away (Plutarch, Pliny). The rival is prosperous — and close. From then on he ends every speech by demanding the destruction of Carthage. 151–150 The Numidian pretext The last instalment of the indemnity is paid. Harassed by Masinissa, Carthage raises an army to defend itself without Rome's consent — breaching the treaty of 201 and handing Rome its casus belli. 149 The ultimatum According to Appian, Carthage hands over 300 children as hostages, then 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults… before Rome demands that it abandon the city and resettle 80 stadia (≈ 15 km) from the sea. Refusal: the city holds out for three years, until 146. Why such relentlessness? The ancient sources themselves give several reasons — all of them Roman. Cato the Elder "Carthage must be destroyed" Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam. "Furthermore, I consider that Carthage must be destroyed." Plutarch reports that Cato ended every opinion he gave with this demand; the famous Latin wording is a later reconstruction. "Carthago delenda est" is the short version. Scipio Nasica Useful fear In the Senate, Nasica replied that Carthage should be preserved: fear of the rival (metus Punicus) kept Romans disciplined. Sallust would later date the beginning of Rome's decline to its disappearance. Polybius The richest city in the world An eyewitness of the siege, Polybius says it was reputed the richest city in the world. After 146 the Senate even had Mago's treatise on agriculture translated into Latin: Rome destroyed its rival but kept its knowledge. Mago the agronomist → Two models face to face Carthage Rome Wealth From sea trade and agriculture From conquest and tribute Army Professional mercenaries Citizen-soldiers (legionaries) Navy Long-standing naval supremacy Fleet built during the First Punic War Government Sufetes, merchant oligarchy Consuls, aristocracy Currency Electrum, gold, silver, bronze Silver denarius The Punic ports today. The circular harbour sheltered the war fleet; the rectangular harbour, trade. label: Africa and its name
title: Africa and its name — Carthage
desc: Afri, Africa, Ifriqiya: how the name of the land of Carthage, present-day Tunisia, became the name of an entire continent.
headings: A culture that travelled more than genes
body: إفريقية Africa and its name Africa For the Romans, Africa first meant the province created in 146 BC on the territory of Carthage — the north-east of present-day Tunisia. Over two thousand years, the name spread to the whole continent. Bardo National Museum, Tunis Where does "Afri" come from? Four hypotheses have been proposed. None is proven; the first is the most widely accepted. Berber · most accepted Ifri "cave" The Afri (or Aourigha), a Berber people living near Carthage. The Berber word ifri would refer to cave dwellers. The Romans are thought to have extended the name of Carthage's immediate neighbours to the whole region. Phoenician Afar 𐤏𐤐𐤓 "dust, earth" In the language of Carthage, ʿafar means "dust" or "earth": Africa would simply be "the land". An etymology that would echo the semi-arid landscapes of inland Tunisia. Latin Aprica "sunny" The Latin aprica, "exposed to the sun", suggested by Isidore of Seville among others to explain the hot climate. Appealing, but now regarded as a folk etymology. Greek Aphrikē ἀ-φρίκη "without cold" From the Greek a-phrikē, "without shivering": a warm land, as opposed to the Greek climate. Reported by Leo Africanus in the 16th century; a minority view among specialists. The journey of a name From a local people to a continent of 54 countries. Before 814 BC Afri The land of the Afri A local people, not a continent. The Egyptians call the western Libyans Tehenu and Temehu. → 814 BC Libyē Carthage is founded Tyrians settle on Libyan land. The Greeks call the whole region "Libya". → 264–146 BC Afer The Punic Wars In contact with Carthage, the Romans call the inhabitants Afer (plural Afri). → 146 BC Africa Province of Africa After destroying Carthage, Rome creates the province of Africa: the first official use of the name. → 1st c. AD Africa The name spreads Pliny the Elder and Pomponius Mela use Africa for the whole known continent, distinct from Africa proper. → 7th century إفريقية Ifriqiya The Arab conquerors adopt the Latin name for Tunisia and its borderlands, with Kairouan as capital. → 15th–16th c. Africa The whole continent With the great voyages, cartographers extend the name down to the Cape of Good Hope. Kairouan, founded in 670, capital of Ifriqiya Ifriqiya A name never forgotten Ifriqiya (إفريقية) is a direct transcription of the Latin Africa. Used throughout the Middle Ages for Tunisia, together with eastern Algeria and Tripolitania, it shows that the name never left the region. Meanwhile Carthage itself, refounded by Rome, had again become the capital of Roman Africa. See also: Carthage lives in Tunisia → North Africa before Carthage The peoples who preceded, welcomed and lived alongside the Phoenicians. 10th–6th millennium BC The Capsians A prehistoric culture named after Gafsa (Capsa) in Tunisia. Probable ancestors of the Berbers, they left many archaeological sites. Since prehistory The Berbers (Imazighen) The indigenous people of the Maghreb for millennia, ancestors of today’s Amazigh. A rich rock art attests to their presence. 4th–1st c. BC The Numidian kingdoms Elite horsemen from present-day Algeria and western Tunisia. Masinissa weighed heavily at the end of the Second Punic War; Numidian cavalry served Carthage, then Rome. 1st millennium BC The Garamantes In the Fezzan (Libya), a prosperous civilisation in the heart of the Sahara thanks to underground irrigation channels (foggaras), at the centre of trans-Saharan trade. An African city Carthage's African identity A blend of cultures Phoenician traditions and Libyco-Berber cultures mixed; intermarriage was common. The resulting Punic culture was distinctly African. Religion Baal Hammon and Tanit, brought from Phoenicia, took on a new place and new forms in Carthage; the influence of Libyan cults is debated. Religion → The Punic language Derived from Phoenician, Punic was still spoken in North Africa until the 5th century AD, as Saint Augustine attests. Architecture Appian describes six-storey houses near Byrsa; Punic town planning adapted to the African site and climate. An army of peoples Libyans, Numidians and Moors fought alongside Iberians, Balearic slingers and Gauls: the army reflected Carthage’s African roots. The army → Farming know-how Phoenician skills combined with local knowledge of soils produced one of the most productive agricultures of antiquity. Agriculture → "The Lady of Carthage", mosaic, Carthage Museum A mixed civilisation A culture from the East, rooted in Africa, open to Greece and Egypt: Carthage was a crossroads. Eastern survivals Canaanite roots Phoenician culture emerged from the Canaanite world after the upheavals of the “Sea Peoples”, around 1200 BC. It absorbed Egyptian and later Greek influences early on. Carthage inherited this blend and carried it west. According to Augustine, African peasants still called themselves “Chanani”, Canaanites, more than five centuries after 146. title: Historic sites and the towns that bear its name — Carthage
desc: From Cartagena to Ibiza, from Kerkouane to Trasimene, all the way to Hannibal (Missouri) and Cartagena de Indias: the places where you can still walk in the footsteps of Carthage.
body: Carthage · Places In the footsteps of Carthage From Cartagena to Ibiza, from Kerkouane to Trasimene — and all the way to Missouri. Punic wall of Cartagena (Qart Hadasht), Spain The places All Spain · 5 Tunisia · 6 Italy · 3 "Hannibal" & "Carthage" towns 14 places shown Spain c. 227 BC Cartagena 𐤒𐤓𐤕𐤇𐤃𐤔𐤕 Founded by Hasdrubal the Fair under the same name as Carthage: Qart Hadasht, "New City". body: Carthage · Punic world Beyond Carthage From Sicily to the Atlantic, dozens of cities spoke Punic and honoured Melqart. Carthage was not alone: it was the head of a network. Tharros, on the Sinis peninsula (Sardinia) 23 cities and sites featured, from Sicily to Atlantic Morocco c. 540 BC: Carthaginians and Etruscans fight the Phocaeans at Alalia (Herodotus, I, 166) 397 BC: Dionysius of Syracuse takes and destroys Motya (Diodorus, XIV) 1758 Abbé Barthélemy deciphers the Phoenician alphabet thanks to the cippi of Malta Alliance, hegemony, confederation? Carthage and the other Punic cities The western Phoenician colonies are often older than Carthage. From the 6th century, as Tyre weakened, Carthage became their leader: it waged war, negotiated treaties and placed some cities under its authority. 6th c. Malchus fights in Sicily, then fails in Sardinia; the Magonids take up the conquest of the island again (Justin, XVIII, 7; XIX, 1). c. 540 At Alalia, off Corsica, the Carthaginian and Etruscan fleet holds off the Phocaeans (Herodotus, I, 166): Carthage stands as protector of the western Phoenicians. 509 · 348 The treaties with Rome close Sardinia and Libya to Roman merchants. The one of 348 is made in the name of the Carthaginians, the Tyrians and the people of Utica (Polybius, III, 22-24). 215 Hannibal's treaty with Philip V distinguishes Carthage, Utica, and "the cities and peoples subject to the Carthaginians" (Polybius, VII, 9): allies and subjects. Debate Sabatino Moscati saw a loose "confederation" that weakened Carthage against Rome. Other historians speak of hegemony, or even an empire, for the 4th-3rd centuries. The vocabulary is still debated. Very different statuses Who depended on whom? Autonomous allies Utica and Gadir, Tyrian foundations older than Carthage, kept their own magistrates and cults. Carthaginian foundations Ebusus (Ibiza), Lilybaeum and Cartagena were created by Carthage itself. The Libyphoenicians Diodorus (XX, 55) gives this name to the people of the coastal towns linked to the Carthaginians by intermarriage, between Carthaginians, Libyans and Numidians. Tribute and contingents According to Livy (XXXIV, 62), Leptis paid Carthage a talent a day. The cities also supplied ships and soldiers. The Greek and Latin terms ("allies", "subjects") are those of the victors; no Punic source describes this system from the inside. body: Biography · 247–183 BC Hannibal Barca The strategist of Carthage Son of Hamilcar, he crossed the Alps with his elephants and spent sixteen years in Italy without losing a pitched battle. Rome never forgot him. Note — Everything we know about Hannibal comes from Greek and Roman authors writing on the winning side. We quote them, and read them closely. Presumed bust of Hannibal — Naples Archaeological Museum 16 years of campaigning in Italy (218–203), as the ancients counted 0 pitched battles lost in Italy ~70,000 Romans killed at Cannae according to Polybius (48,200 according to Livy) 37 elephants when he left Spain in 218 Benjamin West — The young Hannibal swearing enmity to Rome (1770) 237 BC · Carthage The oath Before leaving for Spain, Hamilcar offered a sacrifice. His nine-year-old son begged to go with him; the father agreed on one condition: with his hand on the altar, the boy swore never to be a friend of the Romans. Hannibal himself told the story, decades later, to King Antiochus III. « As soon as he could, he would be the enemy of the Roman people. » Livy, XXI, 1 — see also Polybius, III, 11 Timeline A life in dates 247 Born in Carthage. His father Hamilcar Barca was then commanding in Sicily, during the First Punic War. 237 The oath, then departure for Spain with his father, who built a Barcid power base there. 229/228 Hamilcar dies, drowned while fighting the Iberians. His son-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair takes command and founds Cartagena. 221 Hasdrubal is assassinated. Acclaimed by the army, Hannibal takes command at 26. 219 Siege and capture of Saguntum, an ally of Rome, after eight months: the trigger of the Second Punic War. 218 Leaves Cartagena in spring; the Pyrenees, the Rhône, then the Alps in autumn. Victories at the Ticinus and the Trebia. 217 The ambush at Lake Trasimene: the consul Flaminius is killed. 216 Cannae, 2 August. Capua and part of southern Italy go over to Carthage. 211 March on Rome to relieve besieged Capua: "Hannibal ad portas". The city does not fall — nor does Capua hold. 207 His brother Hasdrubal, coming from Spain with reinforcements, is killed at the Metaurus; his head is thrown before Hannibal’s camp. 203 Recalled to Africa to defend Carthage against Scipio. 202 Defeat at Zama. Hannibal himself urges acceptance of peace. 196 Elected suffete, he reforms Carthage’s finances and institutions. 195 Threatened by his opponents and by Rome, he goes into exile at the court of Antiochus III. 190–184 Naval defeat at the Eurymedon; refuge in Crete, Armenia, then Bithynia with King Prusias. 183 Surrounded at Libyssa, on the Bithynian coast, he takes poison rather than be handed to the Romans. Reading the sources What Rome leaves out Our accounts come from Polybius, a friend of the Scipios, and from Livy, writing under Augustus. Both admire Hannibal, but Rome remains the hero: Hannibal is "cruel" and "treacherous" — charges his enemies laid against all Carthaginians. Sixteen years in Italy with few reinforcements: the faction of Hanno the Great in Carthage opposed the war, and most of the troops sent went to Spain. Hannibal had to feed and pay his army on the spot. The myth of defeat Hannibal never lost a pitched battle in Italy. Rome beat him only by refusing to fight him, then by carrying the war to Spain and Africa. Lost sources Hannibal’s historians Two Greeks travelled with Hannibal and wrote his history: Silenus of Kale Akte and Sosylus of Sparta, who had taught him Greek. Their books are lost; only the winners’ version survives. body: 𐤇𐤍 Hannibal · Tactics 𐤇𐤍𐤁𐤏𐤋 The art of war according to Hannibal Ambushes, terrain, intelligence and encirclement: 22 centuries later, military academies still study his battles. J. Trumbull — The Death of Paullus at Cannae (1773) Two traps before Cannae Winter 218 and spring 217 BC — after Polybius and Livy The Trebia · December 218 Icy water and an ambush At dawn, Numidian horsemen provoke the Romans, who cross the freezing river on empty stomachs. Soaked, they face a rested army; then Mago’s 2,000 men, hidden in a ravine, burst out behind them. Carthage Hannibal; his brother Mago in ambush with 1,000 picked infantry and 1,000 cavalry. Rome The consul Tiberius Sempronius Longus, eager for battle; his colleague Scipio, wounded at the Ticinus a few weeks earlier. Outcome About 10,000 Romans break through the centre and escape to Placentia; the rest of the army is destroyed or scattered (Polybius). Lake Trasimene · 21 June 217 A whole army lost in the fog Consul Flaminius' column files onto the narrow shore between the lake and the hills. In the mist, Hannibal seals the entrance and the exit, then attacks from every side. Pinned against the water, the Romans cannot deploy. Carthage About 55,000 men hidden on the heights in the morning fog, attacking all along the column at once. Rome About 30,000 legionaries under the consul Gaius Flaminius, in marching column, not deployed for battle. Outcome In three hours about 15,000 Romans are killed, Flaminius among them; many drown as they flee. 6,000 men who had broken through surrender the next day. Rome appoints Fabius Maximus dictator: from now on he avoids battle — hence his nickname "Cunctator", the Delayer. Cannae, in three moves 2 August 216 BC — some 50,000 Carthaginians against 86,000 Romans Roman infantry Roman cavalry Gauls & Iberians Libyans (elite) Carthaginian cavalry Water Step 1 Step 2 Step 3 Phase 1 / 3 The crescent In the centre, Gauls and Iberians advance in a forward-bulging arc towards the legions. The Libyans, the elite, wait held back on both wings. This deliberately weak line is designed to give way under Roman pressure. Hannibal and his brother Mago fight in the centre themselves, according to Polybius. ← Previous Next → ~50,000 Carthaginians: Gauls and Iberians in the centre, Libyan heavy infantry on the wings, Iberian, Gallic and Numidian cavalry ~86,000 Romans and allies: 8 legions and as many allied troops, massed deep in the centre, cavalry on the wings 50–70,000 Romans killed, depending on the source 80 senators or former magistrates killed, according to Livy Outcome Total Carthaginian victory and one of the worst defeats in Roman history. According to Livy, Mago poured out before the Senate of Carthage the gold rings taken from fallen Roman knights. The double envelopment remains the textbook model in military academies. Zama, the lesson reversed October 202 BC — Scipio against Hannibal, in Africa Elephants Mercenaries African levies Veterans of Italy Carthaginian cavalry Legions (maniples) Roman cavalry Masinissa's Numidians Hannibal's only major defeat Carthage About 36,000 infantry, 4,000 cavalry and 80 elephants. A mixed army: mercenaries, African levies and, in reserve, the veterans of Italy. Rome About 30,000–35,000 infantry and 6,000–9,000 cavalry, including Masinissa's Numidians: seasoned legions and superior cavalry. 1 Neutralising the elephants Scipio lines up his maniples leaving open lanes. Panicked by the trumpets, the elephants run through harmlessly or turn back on the Carthaginians. 2 The infantry clash The first two Carthaginian lines, mercenaries then recruits, are driven back. Hannibal's veterans hold firm: the fighting is fierce and undecided. 3 The cavalry decides Having scattered the Carthaginian horse, Laelius and Masinissa return to charge Hannibal's rear — the Cannae tactic turned against him. Outcome : Decisive Roman victory. Carthage loses the war and must accept harsh peace terms; Hannibal acknowledges defeat and himself advises the Senate to accept. Hannibal's five weapons The army of Carthage → 01 Terrain A freezing river at the Trebia, a lake and hills at Trasimene: he always chooses the battlefield. 02 Ambush Mago hidden in a ravine at the Trebia, a whole army in the fog at Trasimene. 03 Intelligence Spies and scouts; he studies the character of the consuls and exploits their impatience. 04 Cavalry Numidians and Iberians, fast and mobile: decisive on the wings and for striking the rear. 05 Coalition Libyans, Numidians, Iberians, Gauls: an army of many peoples held together for sixteen years in enemy land. Then → now Taught in war colleges In strategy, "a Cannae" has become a common noun for the total encirclement of an army. body: Hannibal · Elephants · 218 BC 37 elephants against the Alps A great river, snowbound passes, hostile tribes: the most audacious logistical feat of Antiquity. J. M. W. Turner — Snow Storm (1812) 1,600 km from Carthago Nova 37 elephants at the start 5 months of marching 15 days in the Alps 2–3,000 m altitude of the pass, depending on which one 1 famous survivor: Surus 218 BC The impossible made real In the autumn of 218 BC, Hannibal Barca achieved what the Romans thought impossible: crossing the Alps with an entire army and its war elephants to invade Italy from the north. This march of more than 1,600 kilometres from Carthago Nova remains one of the most extraordinary logistical and military feats in history. Henri Motte — Hannibal crossing the Rhône (1878) Stage 3 · The Rhône Make them believe it is land According to Polybius, the engineers built great rafts covered with earth, so that the elephants would think they were still walking on the bank. Once towed, some panicked and plunged into the water — but all of them made it across. On the far bank, Gauls blocked the way. Hannibal sent Hanno, son of Bomilcar, by night to cross upstream; at his smoke signal the army crossed in boats while Hanno fell on the Gauls from behind. Rafts ~15 m (50 ft) wide 4 days’ march from the sea The animal The North African elephant A now-extinct population, smaller than the savanna elephant: about 2.5 m at the shoulder. It appears on Barcid shekels. The rock Fire and vinegar According to Livy, a rockfall blocked the descent; the soldiers heated the rock with fire, then split it by pouring vinegar over it. The riddle Which pass? Traversette, Mont Cenis, Clapier, Little St Bernard… The debate remains open; recent soil analyses have revived the case for the Traversette. The route, stage by stage From Carthago Nova to the Po plain — after Polybius and Livy 1 Spring 218 Carthago Nova Hannibal leaves Qart Hadasht with a huge army. He leaves his brother Hasdrubal to defend Spain. 90,000 infantry 12,000 cavalry 37 elephants 2 Summer 218 Pyrenees He subdues or negotiates with the tribes, leaves Hanno to hold the region with 11,000 men and sends 11,000 Iberians home rather than force reluctant troops onward. 50,000 infantry 9,000 cavalry 3 Late summer 218 The Rhône Great earth-covered rafts for the elephants; a detachment crosses upstream and attacks the Gauls from the rear. 37 elephants cross 4 October 218 The ascent 9 days to the summit: ambushes by Alpine tribes, rockfalls, narrow paths and bitter cold. The elephants suffer on the steep ground. 5 October 218 The pass At the top, he shows his exhausted troops the Po plain below and restores their morale. The descent, on icy paths, is even more dangerous than the climb. 6 Autumn 218 Italy After 15 days in the Alps, the army reaches the Po plain. Base map: Natural Earth. Ancient sites: customary locations. War elephants Carthage's psychological weapon Which species? A vanished elephant Most likely the North African elephant, an extinct population (sometimes called Loxodonta africana pharaonensis), smaller than the savanna elephant: about 2.5 m at the shoulder. Its exact status is still debated. Carthage may also have had a few Asian elephants, obtained from Egypt or Syria. Role in battle Terrify, then strike Elephants were above all a psychological weapon: their charge terrified infantry and panicked horses unused to them. Each was driven by a mahout. Archer towers, common on the Indian elephants of the Hellenistic kings, are doubtful for Carthage’s smaller animals. The bravest Surus Cato the Elder, quoted by Pliny, recorded the name of the bravest elephant in the Punic army: Surus, "the Syrian", who had only one tusk. According to Livy, Hannibal crossed the Arno marshes in spring 217 riding the last surviving elephant — often identified with Surus. The Syrian · one tusk The winter ordeal Surviving the Alps, not the winter Most of the 37 elephants survived the crossing and fought at the Trebia in December 218. But the snow, rain and cold of that winter wiped them out: according to Polybius, only one survived. In 215 Bomilcar landed 40 elephants as reinforcements at Locri; at Zama in 202, Hannibal fielded 80. body: Carthage · Army The army of Carthage Carthaginian officers leading soldiers from across the western Mediterranean — and the largest fleet of its day. The Battle of Zama (202 BC) Who fought for Carthage? Cannae and the Punic Wars → Carthage The Sacred Band Some 2,500 elite citizens, heavily armed, according to Diodorus. The officers were Carthaginian. Present-day Tunisia Libyan infantry The core of the army: disciplined foot soldiers with spear and shield, re-equipped at Cannae with weapons taken from the Romans. Numidia Numidian cavalry No saddle, no bit, light and elusive: harassment, feigned flight and sudden return. The finest cavalry in the Mediterranean. Balearic Islands Slingers Trained from childhood, they carried three slings for different ranges (Strabo) and hurled stones and lead shot. Iberia & Gaul Iberians, Celtiberians, Gauls The Iberian sword — Rome adopted it as the gladius hispaniensis — and the fury of the Cisalpine Gauls who joined in Italy: the centre of the crescent at Cannae. North Africa Elephants A weapon of shock and terror; 80 at Zama according to Polybius. Learn more → Recruitment An army of contracts and alliances Carthage, a trading city with few citizens, did not raise large citizen armies. It combined three resources: the Libyans of its African territory, liable to service; contingents from allied kings and chiefs, above all Numidians; and mercenaries hired for pay in Iberia, Gaul, the Balearics, Greece and Campania. Generals and officers were Carthaginian. Citizens served mainly in the fleet and only took up arms en masse in extreme danger — against Agathocles in 310, against Regulus in 256–255, during the final siege of 149–146. The system had its weakness: in 241 the mercenaries back from Sicily, poorly paid, rose in revolt. The Mercenary War (241–238) almost destroyed Carthage before Hamilcar Barca crushed it. Libyans Numidian allies Mercenaries Carthaginian officers First Punic War · 255 Xanthippus the Spartan A Spartan mercenary hired by Carthage while the consul Regulus was encamped before Tunis. He reorganised the army, fought with cavalry and elephants on open ground and crushed the legions: Regulus was captured and Carthage saved. Battle of Tunis (Bagradas), 255 BC According to Polybius Hannibal's army in numbers Spring 218 Leaves Carthago Nova with 90,000 infantry and 12,000 cavalry. After the Ebro Leaving garrisons in Iberia, he crosses the Pyrenees with 50,000 infantry and 9,000 cavalry; 37 elephants cross the Rhône. Autumn 218 Arrives in Italy after the Alps: 12,000 Africans, 8,000 Iberians and 6,000 cavalry — figures Hannibal himself had inscribed at Cape Lacinium. Cannae, 216 About 40,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry against some 80,000 Romans and allies. Zama, 202 80 elephants in the front line, then mercenaries, Libyans and Carthaginians, with the veterans of Italy in reserve. The Marsala Punic ship, 3rd c. BC The navy Masters of the sea Punic ships were built in series: the parts bore assembly letters, as the Marsala wreck revealed. Rome copied a stranded Carthaginian ship to build its first fleet. 220 ship sheds in the circular harbour (Appian) ~300 rowers per quinquereme 10 ships allowed after 201 The ships of Carthage War fleet and merchant fleet served one aim: holding the trade routes (Lancel). The Phoenician legacy Phoenician galleys and ships, drawn after an Assyrian relief from Nineveh: Carthage inherited this naval know-how. From the 6th c. BC The trireme Three banks of oars stacked one above the other and a ram at the bow: the classic ship of the line, with some 200 men aboard, about 170 of them rowers. Lancel, Carthage, 1992 4th c. BC The quadrireme Four rowers per rowing unit, for a heavier, steadier ship. Pliny, citing Aristotle, credits the Carthaginians with its invention. Pliny, Natural History, VII, 207 The ship of the Punic Wars The quinquereme Born in Syracuse around 399 under Dionysius I, it became the ship of the line in the wars against Rome: about 300 rowers and 120 marines, according to Polybius. Diodorus, XIV, 41-42 · Polybius, I, 26 Merchant fleet The gauloi The Greeks called the round Phoenician ship a gaulos: broad hull, square sail, few oars. These freighters also carried supplies and equipment for the war fleets. Herodotus, III, 136 Small craft The hippoi Boats with a bow carved as a horse’s head — hence their Greek name, "horses". According to Strabo, the humbler fishermen of Gades used them to fish along Mauretania as far as the river Lixus. Strabo, Geography, II, 3, 4 Explorations The voyages Gibraltar From the start, the Punic fleet protected the trade routes and kept them secret: holding the strait meant closing the Atlantic to Greek rivals, the Phocaeans above all. Hanno A fleet sailed along the Atlantic coast of Africa. Some take it as far as the Gulf of Guinea, others much less far: the reach of the voyage is still debated. title: Institutions and society of Carthage
desc: Suffetes, Senate, the Court of One Hundred and Four, the popular assembly: how Carthage was governed, what Aristotle thought of it, and who made up Punic society.
headings: A constitution held up as a model
body: Carthage · Institutions Politics and society in Carthage Neither king nor tyrant: a merchant republic, admired by Aristotle, where two elected magistrates, a Senate and a popular assembly shared power. Punic quarter on Byrsa, built in the early 2nd century BC 2 suffetes elected for one year — the “kings” of Greek and Latin authors 104 judges on the court of oversight according to Aristotle (“the Hundred” in Justin) 1 year term for those judges after Hannibal’s reform of 196 — previously for life (Livy) 0 tyrants and no serious civil strife in the city’s history, according to Aristotle Who governed Carthage? A regime the ancients called “mixed”: a little monarchy, a lot of aristocracy, a share of democracy. Popular Assembly election? (debated) → 2 suffetes Popular Assembly elects → Generals Senate refers disputes → Popular Assembly 2 suffetes preside → Senate Generals report to → Senate Senate supplies judges → Hundred and Four Generals tried on return → Hundred and Four Pentarchies appoint → Hundred and Four Dotted line: uncertain relationship. The diagram reconstructs a late state (4th–3rd c.) from scarce, mostly Greek sources. Executive and justice The suffetes From Phoenician shofet, “judge”. Two magistrates elected every year, whom Greeks and Romans called “kings” for lack of a better word. They presided over the Senate, administered justice and ran the city, but did not command armies. Who elected them — the notables or the people — is unknown. Sznycer; Seneca, On Tranquillity, IV, 5 Oligarchic core The Senate The texts speak of the “Elders of Carthage” (gerontes, seniores). Drawn from the great families, it probably had several hundred members. War, peace, diplomacy: it decided the major questions, and generals had to report to it. Sznycer; Livy Oversight The Hundred and Four A smaller council that only Aristotle names this way (“the Hundred and Four” or “the Hundred”). According to Justin, a hundred judges chosen from the Senate reviewed the conduct of generals on their return. Appointed for life until Hannibal’s reform. Aristotle, Politics, II, 11; Justin, XIX, 2 Little known The pentarchies Boards of five members, mentioned by Aristotle alone. They filled their own ranks, dealt with important business and chose the members of the Hundred and Four. How they worked remains obscure. Aristotle, Politics, II, 11 Democratic element The popular assembly Free men meeting in the agora, according to Diodorus. When suffetes and Senate disagreed, the matter went to the assembly, where anyone could speak against the proposals (Aristotle). Polybius thought it had gained the upper hand by the time of the Punic Wars. Aristotle; Diodorus, XX, 9; Polybius, VI, 51 Outside the suffeteship The generals Military command was kept apart from civil office. Army commanders, drawn from the great families, were elected separately, probably by the assembly. Answerable to the Senate, they could be tried by the Hundred and Four after a campaign. Sznycer; Justin, XIX, 2 Aristotle, Politics, II, 11 A constitution held up as a model “Carthage is thought to be well governed […]. A sign of a well-ordered constitution: the people remain loyal to it, and there has been neither civil strife worth the name nor a tyrant.” Aristotle, Politics, II, 11 (c. 330 BC) — free translation Aristotle places Carthage, the only non-Greek city in his survey, alongside Sparta and Crete among the most successful constitutions: a “mixed” regime combining monarchy (the suffetes), aristocracy (the Senate) and democracy (the assembly). Polybius would also mention the excellent reputation of these institutions (VI, 43). A snapshot, not a fixed model: the value of the text has been debated since Stéphane Gsell, and historians now accept that these institutions changed over the centuries (Sznycer). The philosopher’s reservations Too much weight on wealth Magistrates are chosen for their fortune as much as their merit: a slide towards oligarchy. The highest offices can be bought — and whoever has paid then seeks to get rich. One man can hold several offices at once. Civil peace depends on prosperity: Carthage regularly sends part of its people to make their fortune in the cities it controls. Two centuries later, Polybius saw the Carthaginian constitution in decline: by Hannibal’s time the people had the upper hand, while in Rome the Senate still governed (VI, 51). He also notes that in Carthage offices were bought openly, whereas in Rome electoral bribery was a capital crime (VI, 56). From the 8th century to Roman times Institutions that changed Origins No attested king. Dido was of royal blood, but the legend never calls her queen. The “kings” of Greek and Latin texts were in all likelihood the suffetes. The theory of a Carthaginian monarchy, argued by K. J. Beloch and then G. Charles-Picard, is now rejected by most historians; even in Tyre, kings did not hold absolute power (Sznycer). 6th–5th c. The age of the Magonids. For several generations the descendants

body: Economy · trade, mines, land A merchant empire Carthage was not only a military power: its wealth came from a trading network stretching from the British Isles to West Africa, and from the Atlantic coasts to the Levant. The Punic harbours: the circular naval harbour (Cothon) and the merchant port 700,000 inhabitants according to Strabo — modern historians rather estimate 200,000 to 400,000 300 pounds of silver (≈ 100 kg) a day: the Baebelo shaft, for Hannibal (Pliny) 220 ship sheds for warships in the circular harbour (Appian) 28 books in Mago’s treatise on agriculture Pillars of the economy Trade, land, mines and workshops: the four sources of Carthaginian prosperity. The sea Maritime trade The heart of Carthaginian power: the routes of the western Mediterranean. Control of the Atlantic tin route Control of straits and strategic passages Trading posts from Morocco to Libya, in Sicily, Sardinia, the Balearics and Spain Exchanges with Greeks, Etruscans and Phoenician cities The land Agriculture The fertile lands of present-day Tunisia made Carthage a granary of the Mediterranean. Cereals, olives, vines, fruit trees Techniques described by Mago Large estates worked by enslaved labour Exports of wine, oil and grain Underground Mines The mines of Spain supplied the precious metals Carthage needed. Silver from Cartagena and the Sierra Morena Gold and copper from the Iberian Peninsula Tin from the "Cassiterides" in the north-west Funding the war against Rome The workshops Crafts Products renowned throughout the Mediterranean world. Herodotus, IV, 196 The silent trade Beyond the Pillars of Hercules, the Carthaginians laid their goods on the beach and withdrew; the locals set gold beside them. They went back and forth until both sides agreed, without a word — and without cheating, says Herodotus. Source: Herodotus, Histories, IV, 196 The luxury industry Purple and the workshops Inherited from Tyre, purple dye was made from the murex, a sea snail of which thousands were needed for a few grams of colour. At Kerkouane, on Cape Bon, heaps of crushed shells mark the workshops; the island of Djerba remained famous for it in Roman times. Carthage’s workshops also produced pottery, glass-paste beads and masks, jewellery, weapons and cloth. The shipyards built in series: each part bore an assembly letter.
